newsitem.title: USA: Hilton may need to sweeten bid for ITT.
newsitem.headline: Hilton may need to sweeten bid for ITT.

text.p: Hilton Hotels Corp. may need to sweeten its $6.5 billion offer for rival ITT Corp. in order to secure its place as the world's largest hotel and gambling company, industry analysts said Tuesday.

Late Monday, Hilton said it would pay $55 a share for ITT, which was a 29 percent premium over its closing price on Monday. But by Tuesday's market close, ITT's shares had jumped $14.125 to end at $56.75, and financial analysts were nearly unanimous in saying a more likely price would be in the mid-$60 to $70 per share range.
The proposed acquisition would establish a gambling and lodging empire with 30 casinos around the world and more than 230,000 hotel rooms.
Before Hilton can claim victory, however, it must first win the hearts of ITT shareholders, who have suffered from recent declines in stock price under ITT Chairman Rand Araskog.
Moreover, analysts said Araskog was not likely to walk away without mounting a formidable defence or, at the very least, offering up some tough negotiating.

"Mr. Araskog is a fiercely independent guy," said Marvin Roffman, president of Roffman, Miller Associates, a investment firm based in Philadelphia. "To me, (Hilton Chief Executive Officer Stephen) Bollenbach has fired salvo No. 1, and this is just the beginning of a process."
Bollenbach stuck tight to his $55 bid Tuesday, saying a higher bid would come only after meeting with ITT management.
"I don't think we need to change the price unless we meet with ITT," Bollenbach said in a telephone conference call.

Bollenbach said he would consider a higher price if, after meeting with ITT executives, Hilton determined ITT had greater value. Any price hike would need to meet Hilton's goal of ensuring the deal would add to earnings, he said.

Hilton is keenly interested in owning the full service hotels that are part of ITT's Sheraton hotel group, as well as casino operations that are in unit Caesar's World Inc. Hilton would likely seek a sale of entertainment assets that include Madison Square Garden, the New York Knicks basketball and New York Rangers hockey teams.
Wall Street analysts speculated ITT would have to devise a clever defence to fend off its rival.
ITT may have leeway to use the courts to block a takeover because it is incorporated in Nevada, a state with tough anti-takeover laws, they said.
ITT could sell off hotel assets or mount an acquisition of another company, making ITT a less desirable acquisition candidate or simply too expensive for Hilton's taste.
With a market capitalisation around $6.7 billion, after today's trading, compared with Hilton's nearly $6 billion, ITT also could seek to take over Hilton.
"It's clear ITT has significant resources to mount a defence," said Jeff Logsdon, analyst at California-based Cruttenden, Roth.

Bollenbach declined to discuss possible options or the prospect of ITT mounting its so-called "poison pill" defence until he has had a chance to discuss the offer. As of Tuesday morning, he said ITT officials have yet to contact Hilton.
ITT was part of a huge conglomerate until 1995, when it spun off its manufacturing operations as ITT Industries and its insurance division as ITT Hartford Group Inc.
Araskog has run ITT since 1979 and took over as top executive after the spin-off was completed about one year ago.

But in the year it has operated solely as an entertainment and lodging company, ITT has faced fierce competition and an expensive growth plan in the hotel and gambling sector. As a result, its stock price had eroded to the point where it has become ripe for a takeover attempt.
"(ITT) always buys the best and they've always paid a lot of money for those assets -- maybe too much," said Bruce Raabe of investment firm Collins & Co.
The view that those assets should be contributing more to the bottom line make ITT appetising, industry experts said.
Indeed, Hilton believes it can cut costs by an estimated $100 million by consolidating reservations systems, reducing management overhead and scaling back ITT expansion plans.

"It's economics that compel these things, and we have the opportunity to put together a company that is simply more economical," Bollenbach said in an interview immediatley following Hilton's announcement late Monday.
